rows.sourceExcerpt: A dry-stone wall may look informal, yet its construction follows a disciplined sequence rather than the chance piling of rock. Its recognised profile and finish respond to the size, shape and composition of local stone, so a form familiar in one district need not be copied elsewhere. Before building starts, usable material is sorted into broad working groups. Building stones will form the two visible faces, through stones are reserved to connect those faces, and coping stones are kept for the top.

responseBinding.questionText: Paragraph B
responseBinding.correctOptionText: Preparing a secure beginning below the wall

rows.sourceExcerpt: The first constructed layer is the footing, which gives remaining courses a firm base. Work begins by clearing weak material until firm ground or firm stones are reached and, where the guidance calls for it, preparing a shallow trench. The largest suitable stones are normally chosen for this beginning and are arranged so that they sit securely. Irregular spaces beneath them are packed with stone rather than left to make the footing rock. Fine loose fill is not a substitute for careful placement, and the bounded guidance also excludes concrete and mortar from this dry construction.

responseBinding.questionText: Paragraph G

rows.sourceExcerpt: Repair begins with a decision about where reliable construction resumes, not with covering the most obvious surface gap. Damaged work is dismantled back to sound construction so that the new section can join material that is still firm.
